title: Averages settle down
objectives: See the law of large numbers in simulation, then state it
Show that the variance of an average is $\sigma^2/n$
Tell an average that settles from a count or a fat-tailed mean that does not

screens.title: Three players, one die each
screens.prose: Ann, Ben and Cal each roll a fair die 1,000 times. Each line is one player's average so far. Slide $n$ to add rolls.

params.yLabel: Average of the rolls so far

screens.question: Slide $n$ to 1,000. What happens to the three averages?

options.text: They close in on 3.5, and on each other
They stay about as far apart as after 10 rolls
options.why: You read the left end of the chart. After 10 rolls they spanned 2.6 to 4.5. Slide on and the gap shrinks.

options.text: Each settles on its own number, one per player
options.why: You gave each player a personal number. They all roll the same fair die, so they all head for the same place.

options.text: They reach exactly 3.5 and stay there
options.why: Read the caption at 1,000 rolls: 3.56, 3.43 and 3.50. Close is not equal; the misses keep shrinking.

hints.text: Slide $n$ all the way to the right.
Compare the caption at 10 rolls with the caption at 1,000 rolls.

feedback.correct: The three lines start far apart and squeeze towards 3.5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide $n$ to 1,000 and read the caption.

explain.text: After 10 rolls the averages were 4.50, 2.60 and 3.70. After 1,000 they are 3.56, 3.43 and 3.50. Each new roll moves a long average very little, so the lines settle near $3.5$, the mean of one roll.

screens.title: A lopsided payoff
screens.prose: A scratch card pays £10 with chance 0.1 and nothing otherwise. The line is your average payout per card over the cards bought so far.

derive.caption: After {{n}} cards the average payout is {{money(v[n - 1])}}

screens.question: Where does the average payout per card settle? Give pounds.

hints.text: Slide $n$ to 2,000 and read the caption.
One card pays £10 one time in ten, and nothing nine times in ten. Weigh each payout by its chance.

feedback.correct: The average settles near the mean payout, £1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to 2,000 cards, or weigh each payout by its chance.

byKey.top-prize: £10 is one win. Most cards pay nothing, so the average is far lower.
byKey.usual: £0 is the usual payout of one card. The rare £10 wins pull the average up.
byKey.midpoint: You took the midpoint of £0 and £10. The two payouts are not equally likely.

explain.text: The mean payout is $10 \times 0.1 = 1$ pound. This line was slower than the dice: £0.50 after 100 cards, £0.98 after 2,000. Rare big wins make a payoff lopsided, and lopsided averages need more draws.

screens.title: How close is close?
screens.prose: Call a die average **far** if it misses 3.5 by more than 0.25. The bars are the exact chances that the average of $n$ rolls is far.

state.caption: One roll is always far: no face is within 0.25 of 3.5.

screens.question: As $n$ grows without limit, what happens to the chance of a far average?

options.text: It tends to 0
It levels off above 0, since every roll stays random
options.why: You expected randomness to leave a floor. Each extra roll shrinks the chance again: 0.65, then 0.14, then 0.0000034.

options.text: It hits exactly 0 at 1,000 rolls
options.why: The bar reads 0.0000 only after rounding. The exact chance is about 0.0000034: tiny, but not zero.

options.text: It tends to 0.5, since the average is equally likely to miss high or low
options.why: You split the misses into high and low. That split stays even, but both kinds of miss become rare.

hints.text: Read the bars from left to right.
Each bar is ten times more rolls than the one before.
0.65, 0.14 and almost nothing. Ask where that pattern heads.

feedback.correct: The chance of a far average shrinks towards 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the bars as $n$ grows.

explain.text: A miss over 0.25 has chance 0.65 at 10 rolls, 0.14 at 100 and 0.0000034 at 1,000. Pick any margin, however small, and the same happens. This is the **law of large numbers**.

screens.title: What settles, and what does not
screens.prose: A fair coin is tossed 10,000 times. The top chart is the share of heads so far. After 1,000 tosses there were 18 more tails than heads.

state.caption: Share of heads: 0.491 after 1,000 tosses, 0.4958 after 10,000

screens.question: After 10,000 tosses, where is heads minus tails most likely to be?

options.text: Closer to 0, since the law of large numbers pulls it back
options.why: You applied the law to the count. It is the share that settles; the gap in counts is free to grow.

options.text: Typically further from 0 than at 1,000 tosses
Exactly 0: a fair coin must even out
options.why: You expected the coin to repay its debt. Each toss is fresh, so nothing forces the counts back to level.

options.text: Positive, since tails have been ahead and heads are due
options.why: That is the gambler’s fallacy. The coin has no memory of the tails it has shown.

hints.text: The share is heads divided by tosses. What can the gap do while the share still settles?
A gap of 84 out of 10,000 tosses is a share only 0.0042 from a half.

feedback.correct: The share settles while the gap in counts wanders on.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate the share of heads from the count of heads minus tails.

byKey.pulled-back: You applied the law to the count. It is the share that settles; the gap in counts is free to grow.
byKey.zero: You expected the coin to even out. Nothing pushes the counts back to level.
byKey.heads-due: That is the gambler’s fallacy. The coin has no memory of the tails it has shown.

explain.text: The gap grew from −18 to −84, yet the share moved closer to a half. The share misses a half by only 84/20,000 = 0.0042. The law of large numbers is about the average, never the raw count.

canvas.caption: Heads minus tails: −18 after 1,000 tosses, −84 after 10,000

screens.title: The weak law of large numbers
screens.prose: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be independent draws with the same distribution and finite mean $\mu$. Write $\bar X_n$ for the average of the first $n$. For every margin $\epsilon > 0$, $$P\big(|\bar X_n - \mu| > \epsilon\big) \to 0 \text{ as } n \to \infty.$$ That is what the bars showed with $\epsilon = 0.25$.
screens.question: Which statement does the law make about a fair die?

options.text: For any margin, the chance the average misses 3.5 by more than it tends to 0
After enough rolls the average equals 3.5
options.why: The law speaks about a chance of missing, not about hitting 3.5 exactly. The Ann, Ben and Cal lines never sat exactly on it.

options.text: After $n$ rolls the total is within a fixed distance of $3.5n$
options.why: You moved the law onto the total. Like heads minus tails, the total minus $3.5n$ typically grows.

options.text: After about 30 rolls the average is reliably within 0.01 of 3.5
options.why: You expected settling within a few dozen trials. At 100 rolls a miss of 0.25 still has chance 0.14.

hints.text: Read the formula aloud: the chance of what tends to 0?

feedback.correct: The law bounds the chance of a miss, for any margin you choose.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what sits inside $P(\cdot)$ in the formula.

explain.text: Inside $P(\cdot)$ sits the event that the average misses $\mu$ by more than $\epsilon$. The law says that event becomes rare, for every $\epsilon$. It says nothing about the total, and it never promises an exact hit.

screens.title: Why the misses shrink
screens.prose: Assume each draw has a finite variance $\sigma^2$. We find the variance of the average $\bar X_n = \tfrac{1}{n}(X_1 + \dots + X_n)$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $= \dfrac{1}{n^2}\big(\operatorname{Var}(X_1) + \dots + \operatorname{Var}(X_n)\big)$, since variances of independent variables add
$= \dfrac{1}{n^2} \cdot n\sigma^2$, since every draw has variance $\sigma^2$
$= \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}$, so the sd of $\bar X_n$ is $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$

hints.text: Start by pulling the $\tfrac{1}{n}$ out of the variance.
Pulling out a constant squares it. Then use independence, then the common variance.

feedback.correct: Each line uses one fact: scaling, independence, identical draws, then tidy.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Deal with the $\tfrac{1}{n}$ first, then the sum, then the count.

byKey.add: Variances add only once the sum stands alone. Pull out the $\tfrac{1}{n}$ first.
byKey.same: Replacing each variance by $\sigma^2$ needs the sum of variances first.

explain.text: The spread of the average is $\sigma/\sqrt n$, so it shrinks as $n$ grows. That is why the misses got rarer. Independence did the work: without it, the variances need not add.

screens.title: Put a number on it
screens.prose: One roll of a fair die has variance $\sigma^2 = \tfrac{35}{12} \approx 2.917$.

state.caption: A smooth stand-in for the spread of the average of 100 rolls

screens.question: What is the standard deviation of the average of 100 rolls? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Use the last line of the derivation: $\sigma / \sqrt n$.
$\sigma = \sqrt{2.917} \approx 1.708$, and $\sqrt{100} = 10$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the sd of one roll by $\sqrt{100}$.

byKey.variance: That is the variance of the average, $2.917 / 100$. Take its square root.
byKey.over-n: You divided the sd by $n$. The sd shrinks with $\sqrt n$, not $n$.
byKey.var-root: You divided the variance by $\sqrt n$. Divide the variance by $n$, or the sd by $\sqrt n$.
byKey.one-roll: That is the sd of a single roll. Averaging 100 rolls shrinks it.

explain.text: The sd of the average is $1.708 / \sqrt{100} \approx 0.171$. To halve it you need four times the rolls, since $\sqrt 4 = 2$. Precision grows slowly: ten times as precise costs a hundred times the data.

screens.title: An average that never settles
screens.prose: In the St Petersburg game a coin is tossed until the first head. If that takes $k$ tosses, you win £$2^k$. The line is the average win over the games so far.

derive.caption: After {{(n * 10).toLocaleString('en-GB')}} games the average win is {{money(v[n - 1])}}

screens.question: Slide to 10,000 games. Does this average settle?

options.text: No: a rare long run of tails lifts it again and again
Yes, near £13, where it sat after 1,000 games
options.why: You stopped too early. At 2,550 games one long run of tails lifts the average to about £42.

options.text: Yes, it just needs more games than the die did
options.why: You expected a slow settle, as with the scratch card. Here the jumps never stop, however many games you add.

options.text: Yes, near £2, the most likely win
options.why: £2 is the most likely single win. The average is pulled far above it by rare huge wins.

hints.text: Watch the line near 2,550 and 6,360 games.
Each jump is one game with a long run of tails. Ask whether such games ever stop coming.

feedback.correct: The average lurches up whenever a huge win arrives, and huge wins keep arriving.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide across the whole chart and watch for jumps.

explain.text: The mean win is $\sum_k 2^k \cdot \tfrac{1}{2^k} = 1 + 1 + 1 + \dots$, which is infinite. The law of large numbers needs a finite mean, so here it promises nothing. Some fat-tailed P&Ls behave like this.

screens.title: Twenty trades or two thousand
screens.prose: A strategy's return per trade has sd 2%. One backtest averages 20 trades; another averages 2,000.
screens.question: What is the sd of the average return over 2,000 trades? Give a percentage.

widget.label: sd of the average, in per cent

hints.text: Use $\sigma / \sqrt n$ with $\sigma = 2\%$.
$\sqrt{2000} \approx 44.7$, so divide 2% by 44.7.

feedback.correct: About 0.045%, ten times tighter than the short backtest.

byKey.short: That is the 20-trade figure. With 2,000 trades divide by $\sqrt{2000}$ instead.
byKey.over-n: You divided by $n$. The sd of an average shrinks with $\sqrt n$.

explain.text: Over 20 trades the average return is fuzzy by about 0.45%, more than most real edges. Over 2,000 trades the fuzz is about 0.045%. A hundred times the trades buys ten times the precision.

screens.title: The casino's edge
screens.prose: On a European roulette wheel, a £10 bet on red wins £10 with chance $\tfrac{18}{37}$ and loses £10 otherwise. The casino's mean profit per bet is $\tfrac{10}{37} \approx$ £0.27, with sd about £10.
screens.question: Over 100,000 such bets, which describes the casino's profit?

options.text: About £27,000, and a loss is all but impossible
About £27,000, but a loss is quite likely, as any one bet can go either way
options.why: You judged the whole night by one bet. The sd of the total grows only like $\sqrt n$, while the edge grows like $n$.

options.text: About £0, since red and black are equally likely
options.why: You forgot the green zero. Red wins 18 times in 37, not half the time.

options.text: About £270, because the edge per bet is tiny
options.why: You used 1,000 bets. A tiny edge times 100,000 bets is about £27,000.

hints.text: Scale the mean by $n$ and the sd by $\sqrt n$.
Mean $100{,}000 \times 0.27 \approx 27{,}000$. sd $10 \times \sqrt{100{,}000} \approx 3{,}162$. How many sds is zero away?

feedback.correct: A loss would need a fall of more than eight sds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the mean profit with its sd.

explain.text: The mean profit is about £27,000 and its sd about £3,160, so zero is 8.5 sds below the mean. That is why casinos and insurers can promise steady results from random customers. Many small independent bets make the average reliable.

ideas: The average of many independent draws settles near the mean $\mu$: a miss of any size becomes rare.
The sd of the average is $\sigma / \sqrt n$. Four times the data halves the fuzz.
Only the average settles. The count gap wanders, and a draw with no finite mean never settles.

formula.name: Weak law of large numbers
formula.note: Needs independent, identically distributed draws with a finite mean.

summary.trap: The law is about the average, not the total. Heads minus tails typically grows even as the share of heads settles.

quiz.prose: Daily returns of a stock have sd 1.5%, independently from day to day.
quiz.question: What is the sd of the average daily return over 25 days? Give a percentage.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the daily sd by $\sqrt{25}$.

byKey.over-n: You divided by 25. The sd of an average shrinks with $\sqrt n$.
byKey.same: That is the sd of one day. Averaging 25 days shrinks it.

explain.text: $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \sigma^2 / n$, so the sd is $\sigma / \sqrt n = 1.5\% / 5 = 0.3\%$.

quiz.prose: A fair coin has shown 520 heads in 1,000 tosses. You toss it 1,000 more times.
quiz.question: How many heads do you expect in all 2,000 tosses?

widget.accept: 1,020: the 520 so far plus 500 expected from the new tosses

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first 520 are fixed; only the new tosses are random.

byKey.evens-out: You expected the coin to pay back its extra heads. The new tosses have no memory of them.
byKey.same-rate: You assumed the coin keeps its 52% rate. It is fair, so expect 500 from 1,000 new tosses.

explain.text: Expect 500 heads from the new tosses, so 1,020 in all. The lead of 40 heads is not erased. The share still moves towards a half, $1020 / 2000 = 0.51$, because the lead is divided by more tosses.

quiz.prose: An insurer sells 10,000 policies. Each pays a £5,000 claim with chance 0.01, independently. The mean claim per policy is £50 and its sd about £497.
quiz.question: Roughly how far from £50 is the average claim per policy likely to land?

options.text: Within about £10
Within about £500
options.why: That is the sd of one policy. Averaging 10,000 policies divides it by 100.

options.text: Exactly £50
options.why: The average still varies a little. Its sd is about £5, not zero.

options.text: Within about 5p
options.why: You divided the sd by $n = 10{,}000$. Divide by $\sqrt n = 100$.

feedback.correct: The sd of the average is about £5, so two sds is about £10.

explain.text: The sd of the average claim is $497 / \sqrt{10{,}000} \approx 5$ pounds. Two sds is about £10. That is why the insurer can price each policy near £50 plus costs.

quiz.prose: Each option describes independent draws from one distribution.
quiz.question: For which draws does the running average fail to settle?

options.text: Wins in the St Petersburg game, £$2^k$ for $k$ tosses to the first head
A scratch card paying £10 with chance 0.1
options.why: Lopsided, but its mean is finite, £1. Its average settles, only slowly.

options.text: Rolls of a fair die
options.why: The die has mean 3.5, and its averages settled in the first screen.

options.text: Coin tosses scored 1 for heads and 0 for tails
options.why: The share of heads settles at a half. Only the count gap wanders.

feedback.correct: Its mean is infinite, so the law does not apply.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the draw with no finite mean.

explain.text: The St Petersburg mean is $1 + 1 + 1 + \dots$, which has no finite value. The law of large numbers needs a finite mean. The other three all have one, so their averages settle.
